notes.front: What is trunk-based development?
notes.back: A branching strategy built around one main integration branch, into which short-lived topic branches merge through pull requests.
notes.explanation: Microsoft describes its own release flow as a simple trunk-based strategy, and calls GitHub flow a popular trunk-based development flow.
notes.example: Every developer branches from `main`, works for a day or two, and merges back through a reviewed pull request.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “How Microsoft develops with DevOps”, “Microsoft release flow”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is a feature branch?
notes.back: A branch based off the main branch in which you develop a feature or fix a bug; also called a topic branch.
notes.explanation: It isolates work in progress from the completed work in the main branch.
notes.example: A branch called `feature/invoice-export` that holds a week of work before it is reviewed and merged.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Adopt a Git branching strategy”, “Use feature branches for your work” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Develop your features and fix bugs in feature branches based off your main branch. These branches are also known as *topic branches*. Feature branches isolate work in progress from the completed work in the main branch.

notes.front: What is a release branch?
notes.back: A long-lived branch used to coordinate and stabilise the changes in one release of your code.
notes.explanation: Unlike feature branches, it is not merged back into the main branch in a pull request.
notes.example: A branch named `release/2027-q1` that only receives fixes while the next version grows on `main`.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Adopt a Git branching strategy”, “Manage releases” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Use release branches to coordinate and stabilize changes in a release of your code. This branch is long-lived and isn't merged back into the main branch in a pull request, unlike the feature branches.

notes.front: What is a branch policy in Azure Repos?
notes.back: A rule that protects an important branch by requiring pull requests, reviewers, builds or other checks before changes merge.
notes.explanation: You configure them in the Azure DevOps web portal or with the Azure DevOps command line.
notes.example: Like a branch protection rule on GitHub, but set on a branch in an Azure Repos Git repository.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Set and manage branch policies” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Use branch policies to protect important branches by requiring pull requests, reviewers, builds, and other checks before changes merge. This article shows how to configure and manage branch policies in the Azure DevOps web portal and Azure DevOps CLI.

notes.front: What is pull request autocomplete in Azure Repos?
notes.back: An option that completes a pull request automatically once it fulfils all its branch policies.
notes.explanation: Branches with policies show a Set auto-complete button, and the docs call it useful when you expect no problems with your changes.
notes.example: You set a small change to autocomplete before lunch; it merges on its own once the build passes and a reviewer approves.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Set and manage branch policies”, “What is autocomplete?” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Branches with branch policies configured for pull requests have the Set auto-complete button. Select this option to set a pull request to autocomplete once it fulfills all policies. Autocomplete is useful when you don't expect any problems with your changes.

notes.front: What is a squash merge?
notes.back: A merge option that adds all of a topic branch’s file changes to the default branch as one new commit.
notes.explanation: It condenses the topic branch’s Git history instead of adding each of its commits to the default branch.
notes.example: Twelve work-in-progress commits on a feature branch arrive on `main` as a single commit.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Merge strategies and squash merge”, “Squash merge” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Squash merging is a merge option that allows you to condense the Git history of topic branches when you complete a pull request. Instead of adding each commit on the topic branch to the history of the default branch, a squash merge adds all the file changes to a single new commit on the default branch.

notes.front: What are multiple merge bases?
notes.back: More than one true common base between a pull request’s source and target branches, instead of the single best common ancestor.
notes.explanation: A pull request’s diff is worked out from the two branch tips and their common merge base, the best common ancestor.
notes.example: Like two cousins who share two sets of grandparents: asking for “the” shared grandparent has no single answer.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Merge strategies and squash merge”, “Multiple merge bases” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The algorithm takes into account the last commit in the target branch, the last commit in the source branch, and their common merge base, for example, the best common ancestor. The algorithm is a fast, cost-efficient, and reliable method of detecting changes. Unfortunately, in some cases, there's more than one true base.

notes.front: What is a protected branch on GitHub?
notes.back: A branch covered by a branch protection rule, which decides whether it can be deleted or force pushed and what pushes must satisfy.
notes.explanation: The rule can set requirements such as passing status checks or a linear commit history.
notes.example: `main` in a team repository, where a rule requires one approving review before anything merges.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About protected branches”
notes.evidence: You can protect important branches by setting branch protection rules, which define whether collaborators can delete or force push to the branch and set requirements for any pushes to the branch, such as passing status checks or a linear commit history.

notes.front: What is a ruleset on GitHub?
notes.back: A named list of rules that applies to a repository, or to multiple repositories in an organisation.
notes.explanation: One ruleset can therefore cover many repositories in an organisation, not just one.
notes.example: A ruleset named “hotfix rules” that targets `hotfix/*` branches and requires signed commits.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About rulesets”, “About rulesets”
notes.evidence: A ruleset is a named list of rules that applies to a repository or to multiple repositories in an organization

notes.front: What is a push ruleset?
notes.back: A ruleset that blocks pushes to a private or internal repository, and its entire fork network, based on properties of the files pushed.
notes.explanation: It can look at file extensions, file path lengths, file and folder paths, and file sizes.
notes.example: A rule that rejects any push adding an `.iso` disk image to a private repository.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “reusable text “push-rulesets-overview”” (github/docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: With push rulesets, you can block pushes to a private or internal repository and that repository's entire fork network based on file extensions, file path lengths, file and folder paths, and file sizes.

notes.front: What is a merge queue on GitHub?
notes.back: A feature that automates pull request merges into a busy branch while ensuring incompatible changes never break it.
notes.explanation: GitHub presents it as a way to increase velocity on a branch that many pull requests merge into.
notes.example: Like planes cleared for take-off one at a time, each checked against the ones already on the runway.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “reusable text “merge-queue-overview”” (github/docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: A merge queue helps increase velocity by automating pull request merges into a busy branch and ensuring the branch is never broken by incompatible changes.

notes.front: What three concepts does the Azure Repos guidance build a simple branch strategy from?
notes.back: Feature branches for all new work and fixes; merging them into main through pull requests; a high-quality, up-to-date main branch.
notes.explanation: The guidance heads this advice “Keep your branch strategy simple”.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Adopt a Git branching strategy”, “Keep your branch strategy simple” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Keep your branch strategy simple. Build your strategy from these three concepts: * Use feature branches for all new features and bug fixes. * Merge feature branches into the main branch using pull requests. * Keep a high quality, up-to-date main branch.

notes.front: What three things should the branch policy on main require, according to the Azure Repos guidance?
notes.back: A pull request to merge code, reviewers added automatically, and a successful build to complete the pull request.
notes.explanation: Requiring a pull request prevents direct pushes to main and ensures proposed changes are discussed.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Adopt a Git branching strategy”, “Keep a high quality, up-to-date main branch” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Requires a pull request to merge code. This approach prevents direct pushes to the main branch and ensures discussion of proposed changes. * Automatically adds reviewers when a pull request is created. The added team members review the code and comment on the changes in the pull request. * Requires a successful build to complete a pull request.

notes.front: How should branches reach the main branch, according to the Azure Repos guidance?
notes.back: Only through pull requests that pass your review process.
notes.explanation: The guidance calls the review in a pull request critical for improving code quality.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Adopt a Git branching strategy”, “Review and merge code with pull requests” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The review that takes place in a pull request is critical for improving code quality. Only merge branches through pull requests that pass your review process. Avoid merging branches to the main branch without a pull request.

notes.front: What are two naming patterns the Azure Repos guidance suggests for feature branches?
notes.back: For example `users/username/description` and `feature/feature-name`; others include `bugfix/description` and `hotfix/description`.
notes.explanation: A consistent convention identifies the work done in a branch and can also record who created it.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Adopt a Git branching strategy”, “Name your feature branches by convention” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Use a consistent naming convention for your feature branches to identify the work done in the branch. You can also include other information in the branch name, such as who created the branch.

notes.front: What does the Azure Repos branching guidance recommend for managing long-running branches?
notes.back: Feature flags.
notes.explanation: The guidance links out to an article on feature toggles for the technique itself.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Adopt a Git branching strategy”, “Use feature flags to manage long-running branches” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Use feature flags to manage long-running branches

notes.front: When should you create a release branch, and from where?
notes.back: From the main branch, when you get close to a release or another milestone such as the end of a sprint.
notes.explanation: Give it a clear name that associates it with the release.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Adopt a Git branching strategy”, “Use release branches” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Create a release branch from the main branch when you get close to your release or other milestone, such as the end of a sprint. Give this branch a clear name associating it with the release

notes.front: Each active release branch represents {{c1::another version of the code you need to support}}.
notes.explanation: The guidance also says to lock a release branch when you stop supporting that release.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Adopt a Git branching strategy”, “Manage releases” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Keep in mind that each active release branch represents another version of the code you need to support. Lock release branches when you're ready to stop supporting a particular release.

notes.front: What are the two documented ways to make a fix land in both a release branch and the main branch?
notes.back: Fix the release branch and bring the change into main; or fix main first and port the change to the release branch.
notes.explanation: Bringing a release fix into main prevents a regression in your code.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Adopt a Git branching strategy”, “Port changes back to the main branch” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: One approach is to make fixes in the release branch, then bring changes into your main branch to prevent regression in your code. Another approach (and the one employed by the Azure DevOps team) is to always make changes in the mainline, then port those to the release branch.

notes.front: When porting a release-branch fix to main, why does the guidance say to cherry-pick rather than merge?
notes.back: Cherry-picking gives exact control over which commits reach main; merging the release branch can bring release-specific changes you don’t want.
notes.explanation: A release branch collects changes meant only for that release, so a full merge would carry them into main.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Adopt a Git branching strategy”, “Port changes back to the main branch” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Use cherry-picking instead of merging so that you have exact control over which commits are ported back to the main branch. Merging the release branch into the main branch can bring over release-specific changes you don't want in the main branch.

notes.front: What are the three steps for updating main with a change made in a release branch?
notes.back: Create a feature branch off main; cherry-pick the change from the release branch into it; merge it into main in a second pull request.
notes.explanation: The change still reaches main through a pull request, not by a direct merge of the release branch.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Adopt a Git branching strategy”, “Port changes back to the main branch” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: 1. Create a new feature branch off the main branch to port the changes. 1. Cherry-pick the changes from the release branch to your new feature branch. 1. Merge the feature branch back into the main branch in a second pull request.

notes.front: Why does the Azure Repos guidance prefer release branches to tags for marking releases?
notes.back: Tags add extra steps: people can miss tagging a commit, or forget to push the tag.
notes.explanation: A forgotten tag push can leave the next developer supporting the release from an older version of the code.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Adopt a Git branching strategy”, “Why not use tags for releases?” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Team members can easily miss tagging a commit and then have to go back through the history afterwards to fix the tag. You can also forget the extra step to push the tag, leaving the next developer working from an older version of the code when supporting the release.

notes.front: What two things happen to a branch once it has required branch policies?
notes.back: It can’t be deleted, and all changes must go through pull requests.
notes.explanation: Together these make the pull request the only route for changing the branch.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Set and manage branch policies” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: You can't delete a branch with required policies configured, and all changes must go through pull requests (PRs).

notes.front: In the minimum-reviewer policy, what does Allow requestors to approve their own changes change?
notes.back: The pull request creator’s approval then counts towards the minimum; without it they can still vote, but the vote doesn’t count.
notes.explanation: The setting decides whether the author can be one of the required approvers.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Set and manage branch policies”, “Set a minimum reviewer policy” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Select Allow requestors to approve their own changes to allow a PR's creator to vote on its approval. Otherwise, the creator can still vote Approve on the PR, but their vote doesn't count toward the minimum number of reviewers.

notes.front: Which minimum-reviewer option enforces segregation of duties?
notes.back: Prohibit the most recent pusher from approving their own changes.
notes.explanation: By default anyone with push permission on the source branch can both add commits and approve, and this option stops the last pusher’s vote counting.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Set and manage branch policies”, “Set a minimum reviewer policy” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Select Prohibit the most recent pusher from approving their own changes to enforce segregation of duties. By default, anyone with push permission on the source branch can both add commits and vote on PR approval.

notes.front: What does Check for linked work items do when it is Required, and when it is Optional?
notes.back: Required: a pull request must have linked work items to merge. Optional: it warns when none are linked but allows completion.
notes.explanation: Optional suits teams that want a reminder rather than a gate.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Set and manage branch policies”, “Require linked work items” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: This setting requires that work items be linked to a PR for the PR to merge. Make the setting Optional to warn when there are no linked work items, but allow completion of the pull request.

notes.front: What does the Check for comment resolution policy check?
notes.back: Whether all comments on the pull request are resolved.
notes.explanation: Like the other Azure Repos branch policies, it applies to pull requests that target the branch it is set on.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Set and manage branch policies”, “Require comment resolution” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The Check for comment resolution policy checks whether all PR comments are resolved.

notes.front: Which merge strategies does Azure Repos allow by default, and how do you restrict them?
notes.back: All of them; set Limit merge types to On and choose the allowed types.
notes.explanation: Enforcing a merge strategy for pull request completion keeps the branch history consistent.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Set and manage branch policies”, “Limit merge types” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Azure Repos supports several merge strategies, and by default, it allows all of them. To keep a consistent branch history, enforce a merge strategy for PR completion.

notes.front: Which Azure Repos merge type creates a merge commit in the target whose parents are the target and source branches?
notes.back: Basic merge (no fast-forward).
notes.explanation: It keeps the source branch’s commits and adds a commit joining the two histories.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Set and manage branch policies”, “Limit merge types” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Basic merge (no fast-forward) creates a merge commit in the target whose parents are the target and source branches.

notes.front: Which Azure Repos merge type replays the source commits onto the target branch with no merge commit?
notes.back: Rebase and fast-forward.
notes.explanation: It gives a linear history while keeping each source commit.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Set and manage branch policies”, “Limit merge types” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Rebase and fast-forward creates a linear history by replaying source commits onto the target branch with no merge commit.

notes.front: Which Azure Repos merge type replays the source commits onto the target and also creates a merge commit?
notes.back: Rebase with merge commit.
notes.explanation: It combines replayed commits with a commit that records the merge.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Set and manage branch policies”, “Limit merge types” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Rebase with merge commit replays the source commits onto the target and also creates a merge commit.

notes.front: What does a build validation policy require before a pull request can complete?
notes.back: The pull request’s changes must build successfully.
notes.explanation: Build policies reduce breaks and keep your test results passing.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Set and manage branch policies”, “Set build validation” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Set a policy that requires PR changes to build successfully before the PR can complete. Build policies reduce breaks and keep your test results passing.

notes.front: With the trigger set to Automatic, when does a build validation policy queue a build?
notes.back: When someone creates a pull request, or pushes changes to an existing one, that targets the branch.
notes.explanation: With Manual, users must queue the build themselves; either way the policy judges the build result.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Set and manage branch policies”, “Set build validation” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: When you set the policy trigger to **Automatic**, a build validation policy queues a new build when you create a new PR or push changes to an existing PR that targets the branch. If you set the policy trigger to **Manual**, users must queue the build themselves.

notes.front: Which build expiration setting marks the pull request build as failed and requeues a build every time the protected branch updates?
notes.back: Immediately when <branch name> is updated.
notes.explanation: The docs say it is best for teams whose important branches have few changes.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Set and manage branch policies”, “Set build validation” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: **Immediately when \<branch name> is updated**: This option sets PR build policy status to *failed* whenever the branch is updated, and requeues a build. This setting ensures that the PR changes build successfully even if the protected branch changes. This option is best for teams whose important branches have few changes.

notes.front: Which build expiration setting expires a passing build only if it is older than a threshold when the protected branch updates?
notes.back: After <n> hours if <branch name> has been updated.
notes.explanation: The docs call it a compromise that reduces builds when the protected branch updates often.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Set and manage branch policies”, “Set build validation” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: This option expires the current policy status when the protected branch updates if the passing build is older than the threshold you enter. This option is a compromise between always or never requiring a build when the protected branch updates.

notes.front: What is the risk of setting build expiration to Never?
notes.back: Pull requests that weren’t updated recently can cause problems when completed, because protected-branch updates never change their status.
notes.explanation: Never reduces the number of builds, at the cost of that risk.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Set and manage branch policies”, “Set build validation” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: **Never**: Updates to the protected branch don't change the policy status. This value reduces the number of builds, but can cause problems when completing PRs that weren't updated recently.

notes.front: How can an external service take part in Azure Repos pull request policy?
notes.back: It posts status to pull requests, and a status check policy makes that status Required or Optional.
notes.explanation: This lets tools outside Azure Repos set requirements a pull request must meet.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Set and manage branch policies”, “Require status checks” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: External services can use the PR Status API to post detailed status to your PRs. The branch policy for additional services enables those external services to participate in the PR workflow and establish policy requirements.

notes.front: When automatically included reviewers are Required, what satisfies a group added as a reviewer?
notes.back: At least one person in the group approving (or the minimum you specify, if only one group is required).
notes.explanation: By contrast, every individual added as a required reviewer must approve.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Set and manage branch policies”, “Automatically include reviewers” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Every individual added as a reviewer approves the changes. - At least one person in every group added as a reviewer approves the changes. - If only one group is required, the minimum number of members you specify approve the changes.

notes.front: Which Azure Repos permission lets a user complete pull requests that don’t satisfy branch policies?
notes.back: Bypass policies when completing pull requests.
notes.explanation: It applies only to completing pull requests, not to pushing.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Set and manage branch policies”, “Allow policy bypass when needed” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Bypass policies when completing pull requests applies only to pull request completion. Users with this permission can complete pull requests even if the pull requests don't satisfy policies.

notes.front: Which Azure Repos permission lets a user push straight to a protected branch without meeting policy requirements?
notes.back: Bypass policies when pushing.
notes.explanation: It covers pushes from local repositories and edits made on the web.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Set and manage branch policies”, “Allow policy bypass when needed” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Bypass policies when pushing applies to pushes from local repositories and edits made on the web. Users with this permission can push changes directly to protected branches without meeting policy requirements.

notes.front: What does a path filter do on a branch policy?
notes.back: The policy then applies only to files that match the filter; left blank, it applies to all files.
notes.explanation: Leaving the filter empty is how a policy covers the whole branch.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Set and manage branch policies”, “Use path filters with branch policies” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Several branch policies support path filters. If you set a path filter, the policy applies only to files that match the filter. Leave this field blank to apply the policy to all files in the branch.

notes.front: Can you push directly to a branch that has required branch policies?
notes.back: No, unless you have bypass permissions; otherwise changes reach it only through pull requests.
notes.explanation: Branches with only optional policies, and no required ones, do accept direct pushes.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Set and manage branch policies”, “Can I push changes directly to branches that have branch policies?” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: You can't push changes directly to branches with required branch policies unless you have permissions to bypass branch policies. You can only make changes to these branches through pull requests. You can push changes directly to branches that have optional branch policies, if they have no required branch policies.

notes.front: Does a squash merge commit reference the topic branch?
notes.back: No. It is a new commit containing all the topic branch’s changes.
notes.explanation: Microsoft recommends deleting the topic branch afterwards, to prevent confusion.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Merge strategies and squash merge”, “Squash merge” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Squash merge commit doesn't have a reference to the topic branch. It produces a new commit that contains all changes from the topic branch. We recommend that you delete the topic branch to prevent any confusion.

notes.front: What does the history of a main branch updated only with squash merges look like?
notes.back: Linear, with one commit for each merged branch.
notes.explanation: Contributors can work however they like in the topic branch without the team changing its workflow.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Merge strategies and squash merge”, “How is a squash merge helpful?” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Squash merging keeps your default branch histories clean and easy to follow without demanding any workflow changes on your team. Contributors to the topic branch work how they want in the topic branch, and the default branches keep a linear history by using squash merges.

notes.front: What are two security risks of merging from multiple merge bases?
notes.back: Malicious changes not shown in the pull request can be committed; and changes may not trigger folder-mapped branch policies.
notes.explanation: The first hides changes from reviewers; the second shows changes that folder-mapped policies then fail to check.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Merge strategies and squash merge”, “Potential security risks of merging from multiple bases” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: A malicious user could abuse the UI algorithm to commit malicious changes that aren't present in the PR. - If changes proposed in the PR are already in the target branch, they're displayed in the Files tab, but they might not trigger branch policies that are mapped to folder changes.

notes.front: How do you get rid of multiple merge bases between your branch and its target?
notes.back: Tie them to a single common ancestor: rebase your branch on the target, or merge the target into your branch.
notes.explanation: The docs say multiple merge bases aren’t necessarily bad, but you should double-check the actual changes.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Merge strategies and squash merge”, “How to resolve the multiple merge bases issue” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Having multiple merge bases isn't necessarily bad, but you should double-check that everything is fine. To get rid of multiple merge bases, tie the branches to a single common ancestor by either rebasing your branch on target, or merging target into your branch.

notes.front: What does locking a branch in Azure Repos prevent?
notes.back: Other users changing its existing commit history or adding new commits to it.
notes.explanation: Both effects apply to other users, which is how locking freezes a branch.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Lock a branch” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Locking a branch prevents other users from changing the existing commit history. Locking also blocks any new commits from being added to the branch by others.

notes.front: Does locking an Azure Repos branch stop people cloning the repository or fetching the branch?
notes.back: No.
notes.explanation: People can still get the branch’s contents; they just can’t change it.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Lock a branch”, “Locking limitations” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Locking doesn't prevent cloning of a repo or fetching updates made in the branch into your local repo.

notes.front: A branch creator automatically gets explicit permissions, including Contribute and Force push, which {{c1::override inheritance from the repo level}}.
notes.explanation: They are directly assigned, so they apply whatever the repository-level settings say.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Set branch permissions”, “Set permissions” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Branch creators automatically receive the following explicit (directly assigned) permissions which override inheritance from the repo level:

notes.front: Which branch permission lets a user push new commits and lock the branch, but not rewrite existing commits?
notes.back: Contribute.
notes.explanation: Rewriting history is kept in a separate, stronger permission.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Set branch permissions”, “Set permissions” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Contribute | Can push new commits to the branch and lock the branch. Can't rewrite existing commits on the branch.

notes.front: Which Azure Repos branch permission is required to delete a branch?
notes.back: Force push (rewrite history, delete branches and tags).
notes.explanation: The same permission allows force pushing, which can rewrite history.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Set branch permissions”, “Set permissions” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Can force push to a branch, which can rewrite history. This permission is also required to delete a branch.

notes.front: By default, whom do a branch protection rule’s restrictions not apply to?
notes.back: People with admin permissions to the repository, and custom roles with the “bypass branch protections” permission.
notes.explanation: You can optionally apply the restrictions to them too.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About protected branches”, “About branch protection rules”
notes.evidence: By default, the restrictions of a branch protection rule don't apply to people with admin permissions to the repository or custom roles with the "bypass branch protections" permission. You can optionally apply the restrictions to administrators and roles with the "bypass branch protections" permission, too.

notes.front: How many branch protection rules can apply to a branch at a time?
notes.back: Only one.
notes.explanation: That makes it hard to know which rule applies when several versions target the same branch.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About protected branches”, “About branch protection rules”
notes.evidence: Only a single branch protection rule can apply at a time, which means it can be difficult to know which rule will apply when multiple versions of a rule target the same branch.

notes.front: With required reviews enabled, how can collaborators change a protected branch?
notes.back: Only through a pull request approved by the required number of reviewers with write permissions.
notes.explanation: Approvals from people without write permission don’t count towards the required number.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About protected branches”, “Require pull request reviews before merging”
notes.evidence: If you enable required reviews, collaborators can only push changes to a protected branch via a pull request that is approved by the required number of reviewers with write permissions.

notes.front: What does the option to dismiss stale pull request approvals do?
notes.back: When new commits change the pull request’s diff, earlier approvals are dismissed and someone must approve again.
notes.explanation: Updating the branch, or merging a related pull request into the target, also counts as a change to the diff.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About protected branches”, “Require pull request reviews before merging”
notes.evidence: If the diff changes from this state (for example, because a contributor pushes new changes to the pull request branch or clicks **Update branch**, or because a related pull request is merged into the target branch), the approving review is dismissed as stale, and the pull request cannot be merged until someone approves the work again.

notes.front: What does a strict required status check demand, and is it the default?
notes.back: The branch must be up to date with the base branch before merging; yes, it is the default.
notes.explanation: It may need more builds, because the head branch must be brought up to date after others update the target branch.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About protected branches”, “Require status checks before merging”
notes.evidence: The branch must be up to date with the base branch before merging. | This is the default behavior for required status checks. More builds may be required, as you'll need to bring the head branch up to date after other collaborators update the target branch.

notes.front: What does Require conversation resolution before merging do?
notes.back: Requires all comments on the pull request to be resolved before it can merge into the protected branch.
notes.explanation: It makes sure every comment is addressed or acknowledged before merge.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About protected branches”, “Require conversation resolution before merging”
notes.evidence: Requires all comments on the pull request to be resolved before it can be merged to a protected branch. This ensures that all comments are addressed or acknowledged before merge.

notes.front: What does Require deployments to succeed before merging require?
notes.back: That changes deploy successfully to specific environments before the branch can merge.
notes.explanation: For example, a staging deployment can be made a gate for merging to the default branch.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About protected branches”, “Require deployments to succeed before merging”
notes.evidence: You can require that changes are successfully deployed to specific environments before a branch can be merged. For example, you can use this rule to ensure that changes are successfully deployed to a staging environment before the changes merge to your default branch.

notes.front: With required commit signing on a branch, what can contributors push to it?
notes.back: Only commits that have been signed and verified.
notes.explanation: A pushed commit without a verified signature is turned away by the branch.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About protected branches”, “Require signed commits”
notes.evidence: can only push commits that have been signed and verified to the branch.

notes.front: What does Require linear history prevent, and how must pull requests then merge?
notes.back: It prevents pushing merge commits; pull requests must use a squash merge or a rebase merge.
notes.explanation: GitHub says a strictly linear history can help teams revert changes more easily.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About protected branches”, “Require linear history”
notes.evidence: Enforcing a linear commit history prevents collaborators from pushing merge commits to the branch. This means that any pull requests merged into the protected branch must use a squash merge or a rebase merge. A strictly linear commit history can help teams revert changes more easily.

notes.front: With branch restrictions enabled, who can push to the protected branch?
notes.back: Only users, teams or apps that have been given permission.
notes.explanation: You can view and edit who has push access in the protected branch’s settings.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About protected branches”, “Restrict who can push to matching branches”
notes.evidence: When you enable branch restrictions, only users, teams, or apps that have been given permission can push to the protected branch. You can view and edit the users, teams, or apps with push access to a protected branch in the protected branch's settings.

notes.front: When you enable force pushes on a protected branch, which two groups can you allow to force push?
notes.back: Everyone with at least write permission, including admins; or only specific people or teams.
notes.explanation: Force pushing is opt-in: once enabled, you choose which of these groups may use it.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About protected branches”, “Allow force pushes”
notes.evidence: When you enable force pushes to a protected branch, you can choose one of two groups who can force push: 1. Allow everyone with at least write permissions to the repository to force push to the branch, including those with admin permissions. 1. Allow only specific people or teams to force push to the branch.

notes.front: What does Do not allow bypassing the above settings do?
notes.back: Applies the rule’s restrictions to admins and to roles with the “bypass branch protections” permission as well.
notes.explanation: Without it, those people are exempt from the rule by default.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About protected branches”, “Do not allow bypassing the above settings”
notes.evidence: By default, the restrictions of a branch protection rule do not apply to people with admin permissions to the repository or custom roles with the "bypass branch protections" permission in a repository. You can enable this setting to apply the restrictions to admins and roles with the "bypass branch protections" permission, too.

notes.front: A GitHub repository can have up to {{c1::75}} rulesets, and there can be 75 organisation-wide rulesets.
notes.explanation: The limits are separate: 75 at repository level and 75 across the organisation.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About rulesets”, “About rulesets”
notes.evidence: You can have up to 75 rulesets per repository, and 75 organization-wide rulesets.

notes.front: Who can view a repository’s active rulesets?
notes.back: Anyone with read access to the repository.
notes.explanation: Developers can see which rules apply, and auditors can review protections without administrator access.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About rulesets”, “About rulesets and protected branches”
notes.evidence: Anyone with read access to a repository can view its active rulesets. This helps developers understand which rules apply and allows auditors to review protections without administrator access.

notes.front: If several rulesets target the same branch, which one wins?
notes.back: None: rulesets have no priority, and their rules are aggregated.
notes.explanation: Where the same rule is defined differently, the most restrictive version applies.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About rulesets”, “About rule layering”
notes.evidence: A ruleset does not have a priority. Instead, if multiple rulesets target the same branch or tag in a repository, the rules in each of these rulesets are aggregated. If the same rule is defined in different ways across the aggregated rulesets, the most restrictive version of the rule applies.

notes.front: How do rulesets interact with branch protection rules on the same branch?
notes.back: They layer: all applicable rules from both are enforced.
notes.explanation: Neither replaces the other, so a branch can pick up requirements from both.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About rulesets”, “About rule layering”
notes.evidence: As well as layering with each other, rulesets also layer with protection rules targeting the same branch or tag.

notes.front: What does the Active enforcement status do to a ruleset?
notes.back: The ruleset is enforced as soon as it is created.
notes.explanation: Active is the status that actually enforces the ruleset from the start.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “reusable text “rulesets-about-enforcement-statuses”” (github/docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Active: your ruleset will be enforced upon creation.

notes.front: Which ruleset enforcement status lets you watch what would violate the rules without enforcing them?
notes.back: Evaluate, with results on the Rule Insights page.
notes.explanation: It shows the effect of a ruleset before anyone is blocked by it.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “reusable text “rulesets-about-enforcement-statuses”” (github/docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Evaluate: your ruleset will not be enforced, but you will be able to monitor which actions would or would not violate rules on the "Rule Insights" page.

notes.front: What does the Disabled enforcement status do to a ruleset?
notes.back: The ruleset is not enforced.
notes.explanation: The ruleset stays defined, so it can be switched back on later.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “reusable text “rulesets-about-enforcement-statuses”” (github/docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Disabled: your ruleset will not be enforced

notes.front: Do push rules need branch targeting?
notes.back: No: they apply to every push to the repository.
notes.explanation: They look at the files in a push, not at the branch it goes to.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “reusable text “push-rulesets-overview”” (github/docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Push rules do not require any branch targeting because they apply to every push to the repository.

notes.front: What does GitHub’s default Merge pull request option do?
notes.back: Adds all the feature branch’s commits to the base branch in a merge commit, using `--no-ff`.
notes.explanation: Every commit from the feature branch is kept, plus one merge commit.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “reusable text “default_merge_option”” (github/docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: When you click the default Merge pull request option on a pull request, all commits from the feature branch are added to the base branch in a merge commit. The pull request is merged using the --no-ff option.

notes.front: What does Squash and merge do on GitHub?
notes.back: Squashes the pull request’s commits into a single commit, which is merged into the default branch.
notes.explanation: The default branch sees one combined commit instead of each of the contributor’s commits.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “reusable text “squash_and_merge_summary”” (github/docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: When you select the Squash and merge option on a pull request, the pull request's commits are squashed into a single commit. Instead of seeing all of a contributor's individual commits from a topic branch, the commits are combined into one commit and merged into the default branch.

notes.front: What does Rebase and merge do on GitHub?
notes.back: Adds each commit from the topic branch onto the base branch individually, without a merge commit.
notes.explanation: With no merge commit added, each original change appears as its own commit on the base branch.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “reusable text “rebase_and_merge_summary”” (github/docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: When you select the Rebase and merge option on a pull request, all commits from the topic branch (or head branch) are added onto the base branch individually without a merge commit.

notes.front: With a merge queue, who decides the merge method for a pull request?
notes.back: The queue does; you no longer choose it per pull request.
notes.explanation: The queue merges each pull request itself, so the choice moves to the queue.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About merge methods on GitHub”
notes.evidence: When using the merge queue, you no longer get to choose the merge method, as this is controlled by the queue.

notes.front: Who can add a pull request to a merge queue, and when?
notes.back: A user with write access, once the pull request has passed all required branch protection checks.
notes.explanation: The queue then checks the changes against the latest target branch and any pull requests ahead of it.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “reusable text “merge-queue-overview”” (github/docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Once a pull request has passed all required branch protection checks, a user with write access to the repository can add the pull request to the queue. The merge queue will ensure the pull request's changes pass all required status checks when applied to the latest version of the target branch and any pull requests already in the queue.

notes.front: Which branch protection setting does a merge queue give the benefits of, without its waiting?
notes.back: Require branches to be up to date before merging.
notes.explanation: Authors no longer have to update their branch and wait for checks before trying to merge.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “reusable text “merge-queue-overview”” (github/docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The merge queue provides the same benefits as the Require branches to be up to date before merging branch protection, but does not require a pull request author to update their pull request branch and wait for status checks to finish before trying to merge.

notes.front: How do repository administrators require a merge queue on GitHub?
notes.back: By enabling the Require merge queue setting in the base branch’s protection rules.
notes.explanation: Doing so unlocks settings such as merge method, build concurrency and merge limits.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Managing a merge queue”, “Managing a merge queue”
notes.evidence: Repository administrators can require a merge queue by enabling the branch protection setting "Require merge queue" in the protection rules for the base branch. For more information, see AUTOTITLE. Once you have enabled the "Require merge queue" setting, you can also access the following settings:

notes.front: What happens to a pull request in a merge queue whose required checks fail?
notes.back: It is removed from the queue, and its timeline shows why.
notes.explanation: Conflicts with the base branch also remove it.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “reusable text “merge-queue-reject”” (github/docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: if there are failed required status checks or conflicts with the base branch, the pull request will be removed from the queue. The pull request timeline will display the reason why the pull request was removed from the queue.

notes.front: What does jumping a pull request to the top of a merge queue cost?
notes.back: A full rebuild of all in-progress pull requests.
notes.explanation: Reordering the queue breaks the commit graph, which forces the rebuild.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Managing a merge queue”, “Jumping to the top of the queue”
notes.evidence: Be aware that jumping to the top of a merge queue will cause a full rebuild of all in-progress pull requests, as the reordering of the queue introduces a break in the commit graph.

notes.front: Which event must trigger a GitHub Actions workflow when a pull request is added to a merge queue?
notes.back: `merge_group`.
notes.explanation: The queue waits for required checks to be reported, so the checks must run on merge group events.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Managing a merge queue”, “Configuring continuous integration (CI) workflows for merge queues”
notes.evidence: A merge queue will wait for required checks to be reported before it can proceed with merging. You must update your CI configuration to trigger and report on merge group events when requiring a merge queue.

notes.front: A team keeps several long-lived integration branches and spends days reconciling them. Which change matches the Azure Repos guidance?
notes.choices:
A) Use feature branches for all work, merge them into main through pull requests, and keep main high quality
B) Add a second long-lived develop branch between features and main
C) Let senior developers commit straight to main to save time
D) Replace branches with tags marking each finished feature
notes.back: A) Use feature branches for all work, merge them into main through pull requests, and keep main high quality
notes.choicesExplained: B adds more long-lived branches, the opposite of a simple strategy. C bypasses pull requests, which the guidance says to avoid. D drops the feature branches the strategy is built on.
notes.explanation: The guidance builds a simple strategy from exactly these three concepts.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Adopt a Git branching strategy”, “Keep your branch strategy simple” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Keep your branch strategy simple. Build your strategy from these three concepts: * Use feature branches for all new features and bug fixes. * Merge feature branches into the main branch using pull requests. * Keep a high quality, up-to-date main branch.

notes.front: A developer needs to change one word in an error message. What does the Azure Repos guidance say to do?
notes.choices:
A) Edit it directly on main, since it is too small to review
B) Save it up and include it in the next large feature branch
C) Create a feature branch for it and merge it through a pull request
D) Commit it to the current release branch only
notes.back: C) Create a feature branch for it and merge it through a pull request
notes.choicesExplained: A pushes to main without a pull request. B mixes unrelated work and delays the fix. D leaves main without the fix.
notes.explanation: Branches are inexpensive, and the guidance says even small fixes get their own feature branch.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Adopt a Git branching strategy”, “Use feature branches for your work” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Git branches are inexpensive to create and maintain. Even small fixes and changes should have their own feature branch.

notes.front: At the end of a sprint a team must stabilise version 7 while new work continues. What should they create?
notes.choices:
A) A tag on the latest commit and keep fixing on main
B) A release branch from main, named for version 7
C) A fork of the repository for version 7
D) A feature branch from the last release branch
notes.back: B) A release branch from main, named for version 7
notes.choicesExplained: A mixes stabilisation fixes with new work on main; the guidance prefers branches to tags. C creates a separate repository, which the guidance doesn’t suggest. D starts from the wrong base.
notes.explanation: A release branch coordinates and stabilises the changes in one release while main moves on.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Adopt a Git branching strategy”, “Use release branches” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Create a release branch from the main branch when you get close to your release or other milestone, such as the end of a sprint. Give this branch a clear name associating it with the release

notes.front: A fix merged into `release/7` must also reach main, but the release branch also holds release-only configuration. What do you do?
notes.choices:
A) Merge `release/7` into main
B) Rebase main onto `release/7`
C) Push the fix commit directly to main
D) Branch from main, cherry-pick the fix, and merge it with a pull request
notes.back: D) Branch from main, cherry-pick the fix, and merge it with a pull request
notes.choicesExplained: A would carry the release-only changes into main. B rewrites main with release history. C skips the pull request the workflow keeps.
notes.explanation: Cherry-picking controls exactly which commits reach main, and the second pull request keeps review in place.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Adopt a Git branching strategy”, “Port changes back to the main branch” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Use cherry-picking instead of merging so that you have exact control over which commits are ported back to the main branch. Merging the release branch into the main branch can bring over release-specific changes you don't want in the main branch.

notes.front: Your team wants to follow the same hotfix direction as the Azure DevOps team. Where does the fix go first?
notes.choices:
A) Into main, then ported to the release branch
B) Into the release branch, then ported to main
C) Into a new release branch only
D) Into a tag, then both branches
notes.back: A) Into main, then ported to the release branch
notes.choicesExplained: B is the other documented approach, not the one the Azure DevOps team uses. C leaves main without the fix. D is not a documented path; tags don’t hold changes to port.
notes.explanation: Either direction lands the fix in both branches; the Azure DevOps team always starts from the mainline.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Adopt a Git branching strategy”, “Port changes back to the main branch” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Another approach (and the one employed by the Azure DevOps team) is to always make changes in the mainline, then port those to the release branch.

notes.front: A feature will take three months, and the team fears a huge, risky merge at the end. What does the Azure Repos guidance recommend?
notes.choices:
A) Manage the unfinished work with feature flags instead of a long-running branch
B) Create a separate repository for the feature
C) Keep one long-running feature branch and merge only once
D) Lock main until the feature is finished
notes.back: A) Manage the unfinished work with feature flags instead of a long-running branch
notes.choicesExplained: C is the long-running branch the guidance wants to avoid. B splits the code base without solving integration. D stops everyone else’s work.
notes.explanation: The guidance points to feature flags for managing work that would otherwise need a long-running branch.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Adopt a Git branching strategy”, “Use feature flags to manage long-running branches” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Use feature flags to manage long-running branches

notes.front: In Azure Repos you want `main` never to be deleted and every change to arrive through a pull request. What do you configure?
notes.choices:
A) A tag on the tip of `main`
B) A branch lock on `main`
C) A required branch policy on `main`
D) An optional branch policy on `main`
notes.back: C) A required branch policy on `main`
notes.choicesExplained: B blocks all new commits rather than routing them through pull requests. A marks a commit but restricts nothing. D allows direct pushes when no required policy exists.
notes.explanation: A branch with required policies can’t be deleted, and changes to it must go through pull requests.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Set and manage branch policies” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: You can't delete a branch with required policies configured, and all changes must go through pull requests (PRs).

notes.front: An auditor finds a developer pushed a final commit to a pull request and then approved it. Which minimum-reviewer option stops that approval counting?
notes.choices:
A) Allow requestors to approve their own changes
B) Reset all approval votes
C) Prohibit the most recent pusher from approving their own changes
D) Allow completion even if some reviewers vote to wait or reject
notes.back: C) Prohibit the most recent pusher from approving their own changes
notes.choicesExplained: A does the opposite, letting authors’ votes count. B clears votes on new pushes but doesn’t stop the pusher approving afterwards. D relaxes negative votes.
notes.explanation: The option enforces segregation of duties: the most recent pusher’s vote doesn’t count.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Set and manage branch policies”, “Set a minimum reviewer policy” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Selecting this option means the most recent pusher's vote doesn't count, even if they can ordinarily approve their own changes.

notes.front: You want developers reminded to link work items to pull requests, without blocking urgent merges. How do you set Check for linked work items?
notes.choices:
A) On, as Optional
B) On, as Required
C) Off, with a comment resolution policy instead
D) Off, with a reminder in the team wiki
notes.back: A) On, as Optional
notes.choicesExplained: B blocks merging until work items are linked. C doesn’t check work items at all. D gives no warning in the pull request itself.
notes.explanation: Optional warns when no work items are linked but still allows completion.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Set and manage branch policies”, “Require linked work items” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Make the setting Optional to warn when there are no linked work items, but allow completion of the pull request.

notes.front: A team wants main to have a linear history with no merge commits, while keeping each individual commit from the source branch. Which merge type do they allow?
notes.choices:
A) Basic merge (no fast-forward)
B) Rebase and fast-forward
C) Squash merge
D) Rebase with merge commit
notes.back: B) Rebase and fast-forward
notes.choicesExplained: A creates a merge commit. C keeps a linear history but collapses the commits into one. D replays commits but still adds a merge commit.
notes.explanation: Rebase and fast-forward replays each source commit onto the target and adds no merge commit.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Set and manage branch policies”, “Limit merge types” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Rebase and fast-forward creates a linear history by replaying source commits onto the target branch with no merge commit.

notes.front: A busy development branch updates dozens of times a day, and requeuing every pull request build on each update is too disruptive. Which build expiration fits best?
notes.choices:
A) Immediately when the branch is updated
B) After a number of hours if the branch has been updated
C) Manual trigger with Required policy
D) Never
notes.back: B) After a number of hours if the branch has been updated
notes.choicesExplained: A requeues on every update, the disruption described. D risks completing stale pull requests. C changes who queues builds, not when a passing build expires.
notes.explanation: The hours threshold is the documented compromise that reduces builds on branches with frequent updates.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Set and manage branch policies”, “Set build validation” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: This option is a compromise between always or never requiring a build when the protected branch updates. This choice reduces the number of builds when your protected branch has frequent updates.

notes.front: Any one of four database specialists should be able to approve pull requests that change `/Database/*`. How do you set this up?
notes.choices:
A) Add all four as individual required reviewers
B) Make them optional reviewers for the whole branch
C) Set the minimum number of reviewers to four
D) Put them in a group and add the group as a required reviewer with that path
notes.back: D) Put them in a group and add the group as a required reviewer with that path
notes.choicesExplained: A requires every individual to approve. C demands four approvals from anyone. B doesn’t require their approval at all.
notes.explanation: With a group as reviewer, approval by any member meets the requirement, and the path limits it to those files.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Set and manage branch policies”, “How can I configure multiple users as required reviewers, but require only one of them to approve?” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: You can add the users to a group, and then add the group as a reviewer. Any member of the group can then approve to meet the policy requirement.

notes.front: An on-call lead must be able to complete an urgent hotfix pull request that fails a policy, but must never push straight to main. What do you grant?
notes.choices:
A) Bypass policies when pushing
B) Bypass policies when completing pull requests
C) Both bypass permissions
D) Edit policies
notes.back: B) Bypass policies when completing pull requests
notes.choicesExplained: A allows direct pushes, which you want to prevent. C includes that same pushing permission. D lets the lead change the policies rather than bypass them once.
notes.explanation: This permission applies only to completing pull requests.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Set and manage branch policies”, “Allow policy bypass when needed” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Bypass policies when completing pull requests applies only to pull request completion. Users with this permission can complete pull requests even if the pull requests don't satisfy policies.

notes.front: A branch has only an optional build policy and no required policies. A developer without bypass permission pushes a commit straight to it. What happens?
notes.choices:
A) The push is rejected until a build runs
B) The push succeeds
C) The push is turned into a pull request
D) The push succeeds only after a reviewer votes
notes.back: B) The push succeeds
notes.choicesExplained: A, C and D describe blocking, which only required policies cause.
notes.explanation: Direct pushes are allowed to branches with optional policies when no required policy exists.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Set and manage branch policies”, “Can I push changes directly to branches that have branch policies?” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: You can push changes directly to branches that have optional branch policies, if they have no required branch policies.

notes.front: A team wants main’s history to show exactly one commit per merged feature, without changing how people commit on their branches. What should they use?
notes.choices:
A) Basic merge (no fast-forward)
B) Branch locks on feature branches
C) Squash merge when completing pull requests
D) Rebase with merge commit
notes.back: C) Squash merge when completing pull requests
notes.choicesExplained: A and D keep every source commit. B stops work on the branches rather than shaping main’s history.
notes.explanation: Squash merges leave one commit per merged branch while contributors work however they like.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Merge strategies and squash merge”, “How is a squash merge helpful?” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The commit history of a main branch updated with squash merges has one commit for each merged branch.

notes.front: A release manager can push commits to release branches but can’t delete old ones. Which permission is missing?
notes.choices:
A) Contribute
B) Manage permissions
C) Force push (rewrite history, delete branches and tags)
D) Edit policies
notes.back: C) Force push (rewrite history, delete branches and tags)
notes.choicesExplained: A already lets them push. B lets them set permissions. D lets them edit policies. None of these covers deletion.
notes.explanation: Deleting a branch requires the force push permission.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Set branch permissions”, “Set permissions” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Can force push to a branch, which can rewrite history. This permission is also required to delete a branch.

notes.front: Repository admins keep merging into `main` without the required review. Which setting makes the branch protection rule apply to them too?
notes.choices:
A) Do not allow bypassing the above settings
B) Require linear history
C) Restrict who can push to matching branches
D) Lock branch
notes.back: A) Do not allow bypassing the above settings
notes.choicesExplained: B limits merge commits, not who is exempt. C: people with admin permissions can always push, whatever the restrictions. D makes the branch read-only, stopping every commit rather than making admins meet the review rule.
notes.explanation: By default the rule’s restrictions don’t apply to admins; this setting removes that exemption.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About protected branches”, “Do not allow bypassing the above settings”
notes.evidence: By default, the restrictions of a branch protection rule do not apply to people with admin permissions to the repository or custom roles with the "bypass branch protections" permission in a repository.

notes.front: A pull request was approved, then the author pushed more commits and merged it unreviewed. Which option stops this?
notes.choices:
A) Require conversation resolution
B) Dismiss stale pull request approvals when new commits are pushed
C) Allow force pushes
D) Require signed commits
notes.back: B) Dismiss stale pull request approvals when new commits are pushed
notes.choicesExplained: A only checks comments are resolved. C loosens protection. D checks signatures, not reviews.
notes.explanation: A diff change after approval dismisses the approval, so someone must approve again.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About protected branches”, “Require pull request reviews before merging”
notes.evidence: Optionally, you can choose to dismiss stale pull request approvals when commits are pushed that affect the diff in the pull request.

notes.front: A team wants required checks to pass, but not to rebuild each pull request every time main moves. Which kind of required status check fits?
notes.choices:
A) Loose
B) Strict
C) Disabled
D) Strict, with a merge queue disabled
notes.back: A) Loose
notes.choicesExplained: B requires branches to be up to date, causing more builds. C drops the requirement for passing checks. D is still strict.
notes.explanation: Loose checks don’t require the branch to be up to date, so fewer builds are needed.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About protected branches”, “Require status checks before merging”
notes.evidence: The branch does not have to be up to date with the base branch before merging. | You'll have fewer required builds, as you won't need to bring the head branch up to date after other collaborators merge pull requests.

notes.front: Nothing may merge into the default branch until it has deployed successfully to staging. Which protection setting do you enable?
notes.choices:
A) Require status checks before merging, loose
B) Require deployments to succeed before merging
C) Lock branch
D) Require merge queue
notes.back: B) Require deployments to succeed before merging
notes.choicesExplained: A checks statuses but not deployments to an environment. D orders merges. C blocks all commits.
notes.explanation: This setting requires successful deployment to chosen environments before the branch can merge.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About protected branches”, “Require deployments to succeed before merging”
notes.evidence: For example, you can use this rule to ensure that changes are successfully deployed to a staging environment before the changes merge to your default branch.

notes.front: Only the release team should be able to push to branches matching `release*`. Which setting do you use?
notes.choices:
A) Require conversation resolution before merging
B) Require linear history
C) Allow deletions
D) Restrict who can push to matching branches
notes.back: D) Restrict who can push to matching branches
notes.choicesExplained: B controls merge commits. C loosens deletion. A controls comments. None limits who may push.
notes.explanation: With branch restrictions, only users, teams or apps given permission can push to the protected branch.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About protected branches”, “Restrict who can push to matching branches”
notes.evidence: When you enable branch restrictions, only users, teams, or apps that have been given permission can push to the protected branch.

notes.front: You create a branch protection rule for `main` and change nothing else. A maintainer without admin rights tries to force push. What happens?
notes.choices:
A) It is blocked, because the rule disables force pushes by default
B) It succeeds after a review
C) It succeeds, because no settings were enabled
D) It is blocked only if linear history is required
notes.back: A) It is blocked, because the rule disables force pushes by default
notes.choicesExplained: C and B ignore the rule’s default restrictions. D ties the block to a setting that isn’t needed.
notes.explanation: Every rule disables force pushes and prevents deletion unless you turn those restrictions off.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About protected branches”, “About branch protection rules”
notes.evidence: By default, each branch protection rule disables force pushes to the matching branches and prevents the matching branches from being deleted.

notes.front: An organisation needs several independent sets of rules on one branch, and auditors must see them without admin access. What should it use?
notes.choices:
A) Several branch protection rules
B) A single branch protection rule with every setting
C) Rulesets
D) Branch locks
notes.back: C) Rulesets
notes.choicesExplained: A only one branch protection rule applies at a time. B still hides rules from auditors without admin access. D blocks all changes.
notes.explanation: Several rulesets can apply to one branch, and anyone with read access can view active rulesets.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About rulesets”, “About rulesets and protected branches”
notes.evidence: Multiple rulesets can apply to the same branch at the same time, while only one branch protection rule applies. * You can change a ruleset's enforcement status without deleting the ruleset. * Anyone with read access to a repository can view its active rulesets.

notes.front: A ruleset on `develop` requires two approving reviews; a branch protection rule on it requires one review and linear history. What applies?
notes.choices:
A) Two reviews and linear history
B) Two reviews only; the ruleset replaces the protection rule
C) One review and linear history only
D) One review, because the protection rule is older
notes.back: A) Two reviews and linear history
notes.choicesExplained: D and C ignore that the most restrictive version wins. B wrongly assumes the ruleset replaces the protection rule; they layer.
notes.explanation: All rules from every source are aggregated, and the most restrictive version of a shared rule applies.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About rulesets”, “About rule layering”
notes.evidence: The rules from each source are aggregated, and all rules apply. Where multiple different versions of the same rule exist, the result is that the most restrictive version of the rule applies.

notes.front: Which GitHub merge option adds each commit of a pull request to the base branch individually, with no merge commit?
notes.choices:
A) Merge pull request
B) Squash and merge
C) Revert
D) Rebase and merge
notes.back: D) Rebase and merge
notes.choicesExplained: A adds a merge commit. B combines the commits into one. C undoes a merged pull request rather than merging one.
notes.explanation: Rebase and merge keeps individual commits and a linear history.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “reusable text “rebase_and_merge_summary”” (github/docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: all commits from the topic branch (or head branch) are added onto the base branch individually without a merge commit.

notes.front: On a busy `main`, authors keep updating their branches and waiting for checks, only to be overtaken by another merge. What GitHub feature addresses this?
notes.choices:
A) Require linear history
B) A merge queue
C) Allow force pushes
D) Loose required status checks
notes.back: B) A merge queue
notes.choicesExplained: A shapes history but doesn’t sequence merges. C loosens protection. D stops requiring up-to-date branches, so incompatible changes can break main.
notes.explanation: The queue checks each pull request against the latest target and those ahead of it, without authors updating their branches.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “reusable text “merge-queue-overview”” (github/docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The merge queue provides the same benefits as the Require branches to be up to date before merging branch protection, but does not require a pull request author to update their pull request branch and wait for status checks to finish before trying to merge.

notes.front: After requiring a merge queue, pull requests stall because a required check from GitHub Actions never reports. What is the likely fix?
notes.choices:
A) Add `push` as an extra trigger
B) Remove the check from the required list permanently
C) Add `merge_group` as an extra trigger to the workflow
D) Enable Allow force pushes
notes.back: C) Add `merge_group` as an extra trigger to the workflow
notes.choicesExplained: A the `merge_group` event is separate from `push`. B weakens protection instead of fixing the trigger. D is unrelated to how checks run.
notes.explanation: Without the `merge_group` trigger, status checks don’t run for queued pull requests and the merge fails.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “reusable text “merge-group-event-with-required-checks”” (github/docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: you need to update the workflows to include the merge_group event as an additional trigger. Otherwise, status checks will not be triggered when you add a pull request to a merge queue. The merge will fail as the required status check will not be reported.

notes.front: What does a squash merge keep, compared with a regular merge?
notes.back: A squash merge keeps just the file changes; a regular merge keeps the file changes and the commit history.
notes.explanation: Both bring in the same file changes; only a squash drops the topic branch’s individual commits.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Merge strategies and squash merge”, “Squash merge” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: A simple way to think about this is that squash merge gives you just the file changes, and a regular merge gives you the file changes and the commit history.

notes.front: How do rulesets and branch protection rules differ in how many can apply to one branch, and in switching them off?
notes.back: Several rulesets can apply at once, but only one protection rule; a ruleset’s enforcement can change without deleting it.
notes.explanation: GitHub presents these as ways rulesets are more flexible, while both still protect branches side by side.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About rulesets”, “About rulesets and protected branches”
notes.evidence: Multiple rulesets can apply to the same branch at the same time, while only one branch protection rule applies. * You can change a ruleset's enforcement status without deleting the ruleset.

notes.front: How does Microsoft’s release flow differ from GitHub flow on deploying before merge?
notes.back: GitHub flow deploys each pull request to production for testing before merge; Microsoft keeps merging to main and batches deployments into timed releases.
notes.explanation: With several hundred developers completing over 200 pull requests a day in one repository, Microsoft says a deployment queue would leave them waiting.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “How Microsoft develops with DevOps”, “Differences from GitHub Flow”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: When new changes are pushed, how does Reset all approval votes differ from Reset all code reviewer votes?
notes.back: The first removes approvals but keeps votes to reject or wait; the second removes every vote, including rejections.
notes.explanation: Keeping rejections means a reviewer’s objection survives new pushes until they change it.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Set and manage branch policies”, “Set a minimum reviewer policy” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Select Reset all approval votes (does not reset votes to reject or wait) to remove all approval votes, but keep votes to reject or wait, whenever the source branch changes. - Select Reset all code reviewer votes to remove all reviewer votes whenever the source branch changes, including votes to approve, reject, or wait.

notes.front: How do strict and loose required status checks differ?
notes.back: Strict requires the branch to be up to date with the base branch before merging; loose doesn’t, so needs fewer builds.
notes.explanation: With loose checks, status checks may fail after the merge if the base branch has incompatible changes.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About protected branches”, “Require status checks before merging”
notes.evidence: You'll have fewer required builds, as you won't need to bring the head branch up to date after other collaborators merge pull requests. Status checks may fail after you merge your branch if there are incompatible changes with the base branch.
